overview: The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's nonpartisan watchdog, publishes a yearly report listing areas where federal programs duplicate or overlap one another. This bill requires the GAO, when practicable, to review each public bill that a congressional committee approves and determine whether it risks creating a new program, office, or initiative that overlaps with an area already flagged in those reports. If so, the GAO would identify the new program, the section of the bill that creates it, and the earlier report that flagged the overlap, then send that information to the committee and to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and post it online. The CBO, which estimates the cost of bills, could attach the findings to its cost estimate. The requirement would take effect after a set delay tied to an update of a federal program inventory or the start of a new Congress. As of September 14, 2026, it had been approved by a Senate committee and placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say giving lawmakers a heads-up that a bill repeats something the government already does could help prevent wasteful overlap before it's written into law.
against: Critics say reviewing every committee-approved bill could stretch the GAO's limited staff and slow its other oversight work, and a finding of overlap may not account for why a new program was designed differently.
